title: Chemotaxis in Inflammation
subject: Pathology
summary: Chemotaxis is the directed movement of leukocytes toward chemical signals at sites of infection or injury. Impaired chemotaxis underlies susceptibility to infection in diabetes, neonates, and immunocompromised patients, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Chemotaxis is the process by which neutrophils, monocytes and other leukocytes migrate along a gradient of chemotactic factors (e.g., IL‑8, C5a, fMLP) to reach inflamed tissue.
b: Key steps: margination, rolling, adhesion, diapedesis, chemotaxis.
Clinical clue: poor wound healing or recurrent infections despite adequate antimicrobial therapy.

sections.p: There is no formal staging system; severity is inferred from clinical impact and laboratory evidence of leukocyte dysfunction.
b: Mild: isolated delayed wound healing.
Moderate: recurrent bacterial infections, especially skin and soft‑tissue.
Severe: life‑threatening sepsis in neonates or diabetics with impaired chemotaxis.

sections.p: Impaired chemotaxis can be primary (genetic) or secondary to systemic disease, infection, or drugs.
b: Diabetes mellitus – hyperglycaemia reduces neutrophil chemotaxis.
Neonates – immature neutrophil signalling pathways.
HIV infection – chronic immune activation and CD4 loss.
Malaria, TB, schistosomiasis – cytokine dysregulation.
Chronic steroid use or chemotherapy – marrow suppression.

sections.p: Patients present with infections that are disproportionate to the apparent portal of entry, delayed pus formation, or atypical organisms.
b: Recurrent cellulitis or abscesses.
Poor granulation tissue in surgical wounds.
Neonatal sepsis with low neutrophil counts but normal total leukocytes.

t.b: Is there neutropenia or left shift? Normal counts do not exclude functional defect.
Quantifies migration toward fMLP; reduced migration confirms functional defect. If unavailable, rely on clinical pattern.
Identify hyperglycaemia as a reversible cause of impaired chemotaxis.
Assess inflammatory burden; may be modest despite severe infection in chemotaxis failure.

sections.p: Failure to recognise impaired chemotaxis can lead to rapid progression to sepsis, necrotising fasciitis, or organ failure.
b: Unexplained high‑grade fever with minimal local signs.
Rapidly expanding soft‑tissue infection despite antibiotics.
Multi‑organ dysfunction in a neonate with normal white count.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, optimise host immunity, and provide aggressive infection control.
b: Tight glycaemic control in diabetics – improves neutrophil function.
Antiretroviral therapy for HIV – restores immune competence.
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics early; de‑bride necrotic tissue surgically when indicated.
Consider granulocyte‑colony stimulating factor (G‑CSF) only in profound neutropenia; avoid in patients with active leukemic proliferation.

sections.p: Monitor wound healing, repeat infection surveillance, and address modifiable risk factors.
b: Monthly wound assessment for diabetic foot ulcers.
Vaccination against pneumococcus and influenza in immunocompromised patients.
Education on hand hygiene and early presentation for skin breaks.

sections.p: Impaired phagocytosis and complement deficiency can mimic chemotaxis failure.
b: Phagocytosis defects – abnormal oxidative burst (DHR test).
Complement deficiency – recurrent Neisseria infections, low CH50.

sections.p: Normal leukocyte counts may give false reassurance; functional assays are essential when clinical suspicion is high.
b: A normal CBC does not rule out chemotaxis impairment.
Elevated CRP may be modest despite severe infection in chemotaxis failure.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly spreading cellulitis or necrotising fasciitis
Neonatal fever with poor response to antibiotics

faq.q: Why do diabetics get more infections?
faq.a: Hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil chemotaxis and phagocytosis, reducing the ability to reach and kill microbes.

faq.q: Can chemotaxis be measured in a rural lab?
faq.a: Direct assays are rarely available; rely on clinical pattern and treat empirically while correcting reversible causes.

faq.q: Is G‑CSF useful for chemotaxis defects?
faq.a: Only when neutropenia is present; it does not correct chemotactic signalling and may be harmful in certain malignancies.

exam: A diabetic patient presents with a foot ulcer that is not healing despite antibiotics – what is the next step? — Check blood glucose control and consider impaired chemotaxis as a contributing factor.

In a neonate with sepsis, the white count is normal but the baby is deteriorating – what does this suggest? — Functional neutrophil defect such as impaired chemotaxis; start broad antibiotics and consider immunologic work‑up.
How does IL‑8 contribute to the inflammatory response? — It acts as a potent neutrophil chemoattractant, guiding cells to the site of injury.
What distinguishes chemotaxis impairment from phagocytosis failure on laboratory testing? — Chemotaxis assays assess migration; phagocytosis tests (e.g., DHR) assess oxidative burst.
Why might a patient on chronic steroids develop severe skin infection? — Steroids blunt cytokine production, reducing chemotactic signals and leukocyte adhesion.
When is surgical debridement indicated in a patient with impaired chemotaxis? — When there is necrotising soft‑tissue infection or abscess that cannot be cleared by antibiotics alone.
What red‑flag sign would prompt urgent referral for a child with suspected chemotaxis defect? — Rapidly expanding cellulitis with systemic toxicity despite normal CBC.

Explain why CRP may be only mildly elevated in severe infection with chemotaxis failure. — The inflammatory cascade is blunted because fewer leukocytes reach the site to release cytokines that drive acute‑phase reactants.
